    14. Group actions and Burnside's lemma#

    A necklace is a ring of colored beads, and two necklaces are the same if one can be rotated into the other. How many necklaces have beads, each black or white? Recording the colors at positions counterclockwise gives strings, and Figure 14.1 sorts them into classes of strings that are rotations of one another. There are classes. Dividing by the rotations gives the wrong answer , because the classes have different sizes: BWBW is unchanged by a half turn and has only rotations, and BBBB has only . This note develops the language of group actions, explains the class sizes with the orbit–stabilizer theorem, and counts classes with Burnside’s lemma.

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Recognize a group action, including the action of a group on colorings.

    • Compute orbits and stabilizers, and use the orbit–stabilizer theorem to find orbit sizes.

    • State and prove Burnside’s lemma.

    • Count the colorings fixed by a group element from its number of cycles.

    • Count strings, necklaces, bracelets, grid colorings, and cube colorings up to symmetry.

    Throughout, groups and their notation are as in Lecture Note 14.

    Example 14.7 (Orders of symmetry groups)#

    The symmetries of a regular -gon act on its corners. A rotation moves corner to any corner, so the orbit of corner has elements. A symmetry fixing corner must send corner to one of the two corners adjacent to , and those two choices determine the symmetry, as for the square; so the stabilizer has elements, and .

    The rotations of a cube act on its faces. Any face can be rotated to any other, and the rotations that keep a given face in place are the rotations about the axis through its center. So the cube has rotations.

    The orbit–stabilizer theorem also proves Lagrange’s theorem, stated in Lecture Note 14.

    14.3 Burnside’s lemma#

    Theorem 14.9 (Burnside’s lemma)#

    Let a finite group act on a finite set . The number of orbits is

    Proof#

    We count the set of pairs with in two ways. For each there are such pairs, so . For each there are such pairs, and by the orbit–stabilizer theorem . If is an orbit, its elements contribute pairs. So if there are orbits, , and comparing the two counts gives the formula.

    The number of orbits is the average number of elements fixed by a group element. Large orbits have small stabilizers and small orbits have large stabilizers, and the double count gives every orbit the same weight .

    14.4.4 Black-and-white images on a three-by-three grid#

    How many black-and-white images on a grid of pixels are there, if images that differ by a rotation or reflection of the grid count as the same? The group is , now acting on the cells.

    • has cycles.

    • The quarter turns and fix the center and move the four corner cells in one -cycle and the four edge cells in another: cycles.

    • The half turn fixes the center and exchanges opposite cells in pairs: cycles.

    • Each of the four reflections fixes the cells on its axis and exchanges the other in pairs: cycles.

    So the number of images is

    14.4.5 Colorings of the faces of a cube#

    By Example 14.7, the cube has rotations. They are sorted by their axes:

    • the identity: cycles on the faces;

    • rotations by or about an axis through the centers of two opposite faces ( axes, rotations): the two faces on the axis are fixed and the other four form a -cycle, so cycles;

    • rotations by about the same axes ( rotations): two fixed faces and two -cycles, so cycles;

    • rotations by or about an axis through two opposite vertices ( axes, rotations): the three faces at each of the two vertices form a -cycle, so cycles;

    • rotations by about an axis through the midpoints of two opposite edges ( axes, rotations): the faces are exchanged in pairs, so cycles.

    These account for rotations, so the list is complete. With colors, the number of colorings of the faces up to rotation is For this is , and for it is .

    Problem (Check yourself)#

    Count the necklaces and the bracelets with beads and colors. Count the black-and-white images on a grid up to rotations and reflections, and check the answer by listing them. Count the colorings of the vertices of a cube with colors up to rotation.
